 Euripides’ The Cyclops 63–75, trans. by S. probably in June 1818, may be the direct source
here (‘Nor can I join the Nymphs on Mount Nysa in singing the song “Iacchos Iacchos” to Aphrodite,
whom I swiftly pursued in the company of white-footed Bacchants’, Loeb trans.), although S.’s trans. of
these lines (see no. 172 lines 60–5; Longman ii 378) does not include the reference to Nysa. Dionysus
was born on Mount Nysa (see e.g. Iliad vi 133, where the association with Mænads is prominent, and
Diodorus Siculus i 15, iii 68). Nysa, variously a mountain, city, or island, was variously situated far
to the East of Greece; places were named after the mythic Nysa by adherents of Dionysian cults. S.’s
geography implies a journey from the Indian Caucasus westwards and north towards Athens and the
Promethean temple of line 161 below (see Curran (1975) 91). The details may also recall Paradise Lost
